title: TCP Selective Acknowledgment Options
summary: Proposes selective acknowledgment options for TCP, letting a receiver say exactly which blocks of data arrived out of order. A sender can then resend only what is missing instead of everything after a gap.

plainLanguage.summary: TCP Selective Acknowledgment (SACK) tells the sender which separated ranges of data have arrived, even when an earlier range is missing. The sender can retransmit missing data without resending every later range.

questions: how does tcp know which packets were lost
how many sack blocks fit in a tcp option
subtitle: Tell a TCP sender which out-of-order data has already arrived.

tldr.problem: Cumulative acknowledgments reveal only the next missing byte, so several losses in one TCP window can force repeated round trips or unnecessary retransmissions.
tldr.mechanism: A receiver that negotiated SACK can report ranges of received data beyond the cumulative acknowledgment; the sender retransmits data not reported as received.
tldr.outcome: SACK improves recovery information but is advisory: a receiver may discard data it reported, so the sender keeps data until cumulatively acknowledged.

today: RFC 2018 is a Proposed Standard. It defines the TCP SACK options for selective acknowledgment.

sections.title: Why TCP Needs Selective Acknowledgments
sections.content:
TCP's ordinary acknowledgment reports the next sequence number the receiver expects. If later data arrives beyond a gap, the sender does not learn which later bytes arrived and may wait or retransmit data that was already received.

SACK adds information about received ranges, helping a sender recover when multiple packets are lost from one window.
sections.plainLanguage: A normal TCP acknowledgment points to the first missing byte but says little about data after it. SACK gives the sender a clearer picture of what has already arrived.

sections.title: Negotiating Permission to Use SACK
sections.content:
The SACK-Permitted option is a two-byte TCP option that a receiver may send in a SYN. It indicates that the endpoint can receive and process SACK options after the connection is established.

A TCP endpoint must not send the SACK option on a connection unless SACK-Permitted was received for that connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The endpoints agree to use SACK during connection setup. The permission option appears in a SYN; later acknowledgments can then carry SACK information.

sections.title: The SACK Option Describes Data Ranges
sections.content:
A SACK option contains pairs of 32-bit sequence numbers. Each pair gives the left edge and the sequence number immediately after the right edge of a contiguous range of received bytes.

The option can carry up to four blocks in the 40 bytes available for TCP options. If the TCP Timestamp option is also present, the RFC says up to three SACK blocks fit.
sections.plainLanguage: Each SACK block marks a continuous range of bytes that arrived. The endpoints identify the first byte and the sequence number immediately after the range.

sections.title: Reporting and Using SACK Blocks
sections.content:
When a receiver sends SACK, its first block must describe the data that triggered the acknowledgment, unless that data advanced the cumulative acknowledgment. It should include as many distinct blocks as fit and repeat recent blocks to improve the chance that the sender receives them.

The sender records acknowledged ranges and can skip those segments during retransmission. It must still retain data until the cumulative acknowledgment advances, because a receiver is permitted to discard data it previously reported in SACK.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver reports the newest out-of-order data first and can repeat earlier ranges. The sender can avoid resending those ranges, but cannot delete them until TCP cumulatively acknowledges them.

sections.title: SACK Does Not Replace Congestion Control
sections.content:
RFC 2018 does not define a new TCP congestion-control algorithm. Implementations must preserve the congestion-control behavior they already use, including limits on how much data is sent in response to an acknowledgment.

A retransmission timeout remains a fallback for detecting lost data. When it occurs, the sender must disregard prior SACK information and retransmit the segment at the left edge of the window.
sections.plainLanguage: SACK adds delivery information, not permission to send without limits. TCP congestion controls and timeout recovery still apply.
